subtopic: Talking with parents about marriage pressure
subtype: Approach: values-first clarity before the talk [Thinking]
passage: Saturday night, hostel. Anjali said I'll only get through the talk with my parents if I know what I actually want, so I took a page and wrote it out. Three things I will not bargain about: finishing my degree, earning my own money, and choosing the person I spend life with. Then the things I can bend on: when, and how quickly. Seeing them side by side made me feel steadier. Before this, every phone call turned into a fog where I said whatever came to mind. Now I have a list, and I can say, "I am not against marriage, I only need it on my terms and a bit later." I'll fold the page and keep it in my notebook. Manoj

qa.q: What are the three things Manoj will not bargain about?
qa.a: Manoj will not bargain about finishing the degree, earning money and choosing the person to spend life with.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel after writing the two lists side by side?
qa.a: Manoj felt steadier, since the fog of earlier calls had turned into a clear list.

qa.q: What could Manoj try next before the call, and why?
qa.a: Manoj could practise saying the first sentence aloud with Anjali, because the list is clearer when spoken calmly.

qa.q: How might Manoj's parents see a child who says the timing can bend?
qa.a: Manoj's parents may find it easier to listen, since the child is not rejecting marriage and is offering room on timing.

grounding: A young adult writes down what matters and what could be flexible before talking to parents about marriage.

subtopic: Talking with parents about marriage pressure

passage:
The evening before the family meeting in her village near Champhai, Lalremsiami walked down to the stream behind the church with a notebook. Her mother's cousins had been asking since Christmas when she would settle down. Her friend Irawati, home from nursing college, sat beside her on a flat rock.
'What will you say?' Irawati asked.
'I don't know yet. That's the problem.' Lalremsiami drew a line down the middle of a page. On the left, 'Must': finish my B.Ed. Get a teaching job and earn my own salary. Choose my husband myself. On the right, 'Can bend': when, maybe in two or three years. Meeting a boy the family likes, if nobody pushes.
She read it back twice. 'I thought I was just saying no to everything. I'm not. It's three things.'
Irawati nodded. 'Then say the three things. Calmly.'
The stream was loud. Lalremsiami tore the page out and folded it into her pocket for the morning.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami write under 'Can bend'?
qa.a: When, maybe in two or three years, and meeting a boy the family likes, if nobody pushes.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel on reading the list back?
qa.a: She felt relieved and clearer, seeing she wasn't refusing everything, only holding on to three things.

qa.q: What could Lalremsiami add to prepare for the meeting?
qa.a: A sentence acknowledging that the family asks out of care, said before the three must-haves.

qa.q: How might the mother's cousins hear the 'Can bend' part at the meeting?
qa.a: They may feel reassured that Lalremsiami is open to marriage in time, which could make them push less.

grounding: Shows a young adult writing what must stay, a degree, her own salary and choosing a partner, and what can bend, like timing, before a family talk.
